title: Atomic MathReasoner: Instance-Level Composition of Atomic Reasoning Skills for Mathematical LLMs
authors: Jiashu Li, Tianyu Gao, Qinglong Liu, Jinping Wang, Ye Wei, Zhiqiang Gao
abstract: Most existing approaches enhance mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs) as a monolithic capability, despite the fact that different mathematical problems require different reasoning skills. Recent work has explored a more fine-grained perspective by decomposing mathematical reasoning into atomic skills and developing specialized modules for individual capabilities. However, how to effectively utilize these atomic abilities remains underexplored. To address this challenge, we propose Atomic MathReasoner (AMR), an instance-level framework for composing atomic reasoning skills. AMR first trains a library of capability-specific LoRA experts and performs gradient-free optimization over held-out validation subsets to discover a diverse set of low-loss composition prototypes. It evaluates the preference of each prototype using the token-level negative log-likelihood of reference solutions, filters ambiguous assignments through a confidence margin, and distills the resulting pseudo-labels into a lightweight router. During inference, the router selects an appropriate composition prototype for each problem, enabling problem-specific utilization of atomic skills without costly online optimization. Experiments on the AtomicMath benchmark across general and mathematics-specialized LLMs demonstrate consistent improvements. On Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B, AMR increases average field accuracy from 64.4% to 68.1% at Level 1 and from 59.3% to 63.7% at Level 2, while improving average logical reasoning performance from 39.4% to 46.8%. These results demonstrate that effectively composing specialized atomic skills provides a promising approach to strengthening mathematical reasoning in LLMs.

infographic.key_insight: Atomic MathReasoner improves mathematical reasoning by selecting a problem-specific composition of specialized atomic-skill LoRA experts.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A lightweight router enables adaptive expert composition at inference without costly online optimization.
method: Train capability-specific LoRA experts and use gradient-free optimization to discover low-loss composition prototypes.

Distill prototype assignments into a lightweight router for problem-specific inference.

infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond AtomicMath and the computational cost of offline prototype discovery are not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Atomic MathReasoner: Instance-Level Composition of Atomic Reasoning Skills for Mathematical LLMs

title: A Systematic Analysis of a Small Optimal Subspace for Physics-Informed Neural Networks: $n$-DAS $\subset \mathbb{R}^p$
authors: Ahmad AliAhmad, Khemraj Shukla
abstract: The search for a low-dimensional subspace that governs neural network training has been a persistent goal in optimization. Yet subspaces defined by Hessian eigenvalue magnitude, such as the dominant/bulk decomposition underlying Dom-SGD and Bulk-SGD, have repeatedly failed to capture where optimization takes place, and adaptive Krylov-based alternatives built on energy-fraction thresholds show promise but still struggle at lower eigenmodes. We argue this failure is structural: the directions of highest curvature are not, in general, the directions along which training moves. We introduce the dominant aligned subspace (DAS), constructed from a full eigendecomposition of the Hessian but selected by gradient alignment rather than eigenvalue magnitude, as a tool for understanding optimization dynamics and a foundation for designing methods that exploit them. To expose this structure under the hardest conditions, we use physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) as a testbed: differential operators from the parabolic, elliptic, and hyperbolic classes induce severely ill-conditioned, anisotropic loss landscapes. Across Poisson, heat, wave, and viscous Burgers benchmarks DAS-restricted training with a line search matches full-space training even where the projected Hessian remains ill-conditioned, showing empirically that convergence does not require all Hessian eigendirections but only a low-dimensional, gradient-aligned subset. We extend the analysis to Gauss-Newton within the DAS and discuss what this structure implies for future subspace-aware optimizers.

infographic.key_insight: PINN training can match full-space optimization within a small Hessian eigensubspace selected by gradient alignment rather than eigenvalue magnitude.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Gradient-aligned subspaces could guide more targeted optimizers for ill-conditioned PDE learning problems without requiring well-conditioned projected curvature.
method: Compute a full Hessian eigendecomposition.
Select the dominant aligned subspace (DAS) by gradient alignment, not curvature magnitude.
Restrict training to DAS with line search and extend the analysis to Gauss–Newton.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across Poisson, heat, wave, and viscous Burgers benchmarks, DAS-restricted training empirically matches full-space training even when the projected Hessian remains ill-conditioned.
infographic.watch_item: Full Hessian eigendecomposition is costly at scale, and the abstract does not establish computational savings or generalization beyond the tested PINNs.
infographic.paper_title: A Systematic Analysis of a Small Optimal Subspace for Physics-Informed Neural Networks: $n$-DAS $\subset \mathbb{R}^p$

title: Structural functional identifiability of unknown differential equation observation maps
authors: Torkel E Loman, Alexander P Browning, Ruth E Baker
abstract: In many differential equation models of real-world systems, the mechanistic structure of the dynamics is known, but the map from the dynamics to the observations is not. This is potentially problematic, as it can prevent us from e.g. learning model parameter values from data. Examples where this occurs include measuring a fluorescent marker as a proxy for the dynamics of a cellular circuit, and using wastewater measurements to follow the development of an epidemic. The nascent field of hybrid modelling, in which machine learning components (like neural networks) are embedded within mechanistic models, provides the tools to learn such maps. Here, the system's dynamics keep their mechanistic form, while a neural network represents the unknown observation map and is trained alongside any unknown core system parameters. This raises a question of identifiability: when can the true observation map be learnt, and when does one simply learn some map that transforms the dynamics into the available data? Building on previous work, we show how structural functional identifiability analysis can establish whether a model's unknown observation maps and core system parameters are identifiable, i.e. can be uniquely learnt from data. We both prove general results on when models with unknown observation maps are, and are not, identifiable, and demonstrate a general methodology (based on differential algebra) for assessing the identifiability of such models. This paves the way for applying classic differential equation workflows to the many real-world systems that contain such unknown maps.

infographic.key_insight: Structural functional identifiability analysis can determine whether unknown observation maps and mechanistic model parameters can be uniquely learned from data.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This helps assess whether hybrid differential equation models recover meaningful sensor-to-state relationships rather than merely fit observed outputs.
method: Represent unknown observation maps with neural networks while retaining mechanistic dynamics.
Use differential algebra to assess identifiability of observation maps and core parameters.
Prove general conditions for identifiability and non-identifiability.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical results and a general analysis methodology, but provides no dataset details or quantitative evaluation metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Structural identifiability does not guarantee reliable recovery from finite, noisy data or successful neural network training.
infographic.paper_title: Structural functional identifiability of unknown differential equation observation maps

title: Stability of Parallel Transport Convolution under Riemannian Metric Perturbations
authors: Hongnian Huang, Andrew Stump
abstract: Geometric convolutions on Riemannian manifolds depend on the geometry of the underlying domain, making stability under metric perturbations a fundamental question in geometric deep learning. This paper studies this question for parallel transport convolution through methods from differential geometry and analysis. On a fixed compact manifold, we establish that, for a continuous input signal and a continuous reference kernel supported in a sufficiently small normal neighborhood, the convolution output depends continuously in $L^2$ on the Riemannian metric in the $C^2$-topology, under the specified localization and transport-path conventions. The analysis develops perturbation estimates for geodesics, parallel transport, Jacobi fields, and exponential maps, and uses these estimates to compare the transported kernels. A central difficulty is the cut locus, which obstructs uniform comparison of the transport construction over the entire manifold. We address this difficulty by combining uniform estimates away from the cut locus with integral bounds on neighborhoods of arbitrarily small volume, while also controlling the change in the Riemannian volume measure. The resulting qualitative stability theorem connects perturbation theory for Riemannian geometric constructions with the analysis of spatial convolution operators in geometric deep learning.

infographic.key_insight: On a fixed compact manifold, parallel transport convolution is continuous in L² under C² perturbations of the Riemannian metric, subject to the stated localization and transport-path conventions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The theorem supports robustness to small geometric changes in manifold-based convolution models, but does not provide numerical error rates.
method: Bound perturbations of geodesics, parallel transport, Jacobi fields, and exponential maps.
Compare transported kernels using uniform estimates away from the cut locus and integral bounds near it.
Control changes in the Riemannian volume measure.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a qualitative mathematical stability theorem, not empirical benchmarks or numerical evaluations.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantee assumes continuous signals and kernels localized to a sufficiently small normal neighborhood; discretized implementations require separate validation.
infographic.paper_title: Stability of Parallel Transport Convolution under Riemannian Metric Perturbations

title: Large-Scale Tensor Trace-Ratio Problem: Randomized Algorithm and Sparse Multilinear Discriminant Analysis via Closed-Form Solution
authors: Yuhang Li, Gang Wu
abstract: Trace-ratio optimization problems from high-dimensional tensor data appear across numerous research domains including machine learning, signal processing, as well as pattern recognition. Up to now, analytical closed-form expressions remain unavailable for tensor trace-ratio tasks; prevailing techniques mostly adopt inner-outer iterative schemes to tackle such optimization tasks. However, when dealing with high-dimensional tensor data sets, existing multilinear discriminant analysis methods often encounter limitations such as heavy computational costs, insufficient memory space, and interference from redundant features. This paper yields two core contributions.First, we present a closed-form solution under the full row rank condition, and construct a randomized solver targeting large-scale tensor trace-ratio optimization. In contrast to prior approaches, the devised algorithm achieves substantial computational speedup.Its core mechanism is to reformulate the original large-scale tensor trace-ratio optimization into a tensor least-squares formulation, instead of the much more complicated (generalized) tensor eigenproblems. We derive theoretical error-bound results which verify the reliability of the newly developed algorithm. Second, we build a sparse multilinear discriminant analysis model leveraging the above closed-form result combined with tensor \ell_{2,0}-norm regularization, and propose a sparse multilinear discriminant method for tensor feature selection. The sparse method can identify key discriminative features from high-dimensional data and suppress redundant information. Comprehensive numerical evaluations are conducted over multiple publicly available real-world benchmarks.The proposed methods demonstrate significant advantages in computational efficiency and scalability for large-scale problems, while achieving competitive classification accuracy on some datasets.

infographic.key_insight: Under a full row rank condition, a closed-form solution recasts tensor trace-ratio optimization as tensor least squares, enabling a randomized large-scale solver.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach targets computational and memory bottlenecks in high-dimensional tensor learning while supporting discriminative feature selection.
method: Replace generalized tensor eigenproblems with a tensor least-squares formulation.
Develop a randomized solver with theoretical error bounds.
Combine the closed-form result with tensor ℓ₂,₀ regularization for sparse multilinear discriminant analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations on multiple public real-world benchmarks report efficiency and scalability advantages, with competitive classification accuracy on some datasets.
infographic.watch_item: The closed-form result requires full row rank; applicability to rank-deficient data needs verification.
infographic.paper_title: Large-Scale Tensor Trace-Ratio Problem: Randomized Algorithm and Sparse Multilinear Discriminant Analysis via Closed-Form Solution

title: Balancing Exploration and Exploitation in Constrained Combinatorial Optimization with U(1)-Symmetric Tensor Trains
authors: Sergei Iudin, Mikhail Podobrii, Dmitry Zheltkov, Stanislav Moiseev
abstract: Tensor Train (TT) decomposition has emerged as a powerful tool for mitigating the curse of dimensionality in a variety of machine learning and combinatorial optimization tasks. Recent advances show that TT-based generative models can efficiently represent and explore high-dimensional discrete spaces, even when the cost function structure is unknown. However, incorporating hard linear constraints into TT-based optimization remains challenging, as existing interpolation and sampling approaches often fail when feasible points are rare. In this work, we develop a general TT-based framework for constrained combinatorial optimization built upon U(1)-symmetric tensor networks. Our method introduces an expressibility-enhancement mechanism for constructing sparse symmetric tensors and a graph-based diversity measure that guides sample selection during training. On assignment benchmarks, expressibility enhancement and diversity-aware selection improve mean solution quality over their respective baselines. The assignment-selected diversifying strategy also extends to nonpolynomial Set Partitioning, with larger relative gains observed in the higher-tensor-rank data families. Separate runtime benchmarks show substantial speedups over ConstrainTNet and PROTES on non-degenerate assignment workloads; comparisons with simulated annealing depend on constraint information and computational budget, but, overall, support the practicality of the current implementation.

infographic.key_insight: U(1)-symmetric tensor trains support hard-constrained combinatorial search while balancing model expressibility and sampling diversity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a practical approach to assignment and set-partitioning problems where feasible solutions are rare.
method: Encode hard linear constraints using U(1)-symmetric tensor networks.
Enhance the expressibility of sparse symmetric tensors.
Use a graph-based diversity measure to guide training-sample selection.
infographic.evidence_signal: Assignment benchmarks show improved mean solution quality, Set Partitioning tests show larger relative gains in higher-rank data families, and separate runtime tests show substantial speedups over ConstrainTNet and PROTES on non-degenerate assignments.
infographic.watch_item: Performance relative to simulated annealing depends on available constraint information and computational budget.
infographic.paper_title: Balancing Exploration and Exploitation in Constrained Combinatorial Optimization with U(1)-Symmetric Tensor Trains

title: Turing Agent: Agentic Formal Verification for Mathematical Research
authors: Yang Chen, Qianyi Wang, Ronghui Yang, Zhanhao Li, Yu Cong, Chen Zhang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly advancing mathematical discovery, moving beyond benchmark-level problem solving to tackle frontier research problems. This progress is ushering mathematics into an era of proof abundance, raising a fundamental challenge: how can we ensure the correctness of the ever-growing volume of AI-generated proofs and transform them into trustworthy, machine-verified mathematical knowledge? We introduce Turing Agent, an agent harness designed to orchestrate end-to-end formal verification of research-level mathematics. Its wo-scale architecture integrates theorem formalization and proof formalization agents, empowered by structured proof decomposition, parallel verification, accumulated proof experience, and selective semantic review. Leveraging our collaborations with theoretical computer science (TCS) researchers, we focus our evaluation on TCS, a particularly demanding domain characterized by intricate quantification, complex dependencies, and stringent semantic requirements. Against direct generation and general-purpose coding harnesses, including Codex CLI and Claude Code, Turing Agent achieves approximately 57-62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench and 83% overall pass@1 on a TCS-focused subset of RLMEval, using GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Notably, Turing Agent, built on DeepSeek, successfully completes the formal verification of three previously unresolved TCS tasks from OpenAI's October 2026 collection. One particularly challenging TCS problem required about a hundred formally verified auxiliary claims. Moreover, by actively exploring and refining the formalization process, Turing Agent can uncover simpler alternative proofs, expose unnecessary dependencies in original proofs, and generate reusable mathematical knowledge as a byproduct of verification.

infographic.key_insight: Turing Agent coordinates theorem and proof formalization to turn research-level mathematical arguments into machine-verified knowledge.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its specialized verification workflow offers a model for building AI systems that produce checkable technical results rather than plausible text alone.
method: Use a two-scale architecture with theorem and proof formalization agents.
Decompose proofs into structured claims and verify them in parallel.
Reuse accumulated proof experience and selectively review semantic fidelity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports approximately 57–62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench and 83% overall pass@1 on a TCS-focused RLMEval subset using GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro.
infographic.watch_item: Formal proof acceptance does not alone establish fidelity to the intended theorem; semantic review remains important, and evaluation focuses on theoretical computer science.
infographic.paper_title: Turing Agent: Agentic Formal Verification for Mathematical Research

title: CurvDelta: Low-Curvature Delta Modeling For Surgical Learning and Unlearning
authors: Zeguan Xiao, Zhuocheng Liang, Yun Chen, Yong Wang, Guanhua Chen, Pinyan Lu
abstract: A central challenge in adapting large language models (LLMs) is capability preservation: an adaptation can achieve its target while degrading general capabilities. We introduce CurvDelta, a scalable framework that incorporates the preservation constraint into the parameterization of the model update. By analyzing the local geometry of the preservation constraint around the pre-adaptation model, CurvDelta constructs a low-curvature space in which parameter updates leave the preservation loss nearly invariant. We make its construction practical for LLMs through Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC) and a factorized projection. We also introduce CurvLoRA, a low-rank variant within the same preservation geometry, designed for more efficient adaptation. Both methods apply to preservation-constrained adaptation tasks such as capability learning and selective unlearning. We evaluate our methods on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge unlearning. For mathematical reasoning and code generation, our approaches achieve competitive downstream performance while better preserving general capabilities, offering a favorable acquisition--retention trade-off relative to the baselines. For knowledge unlearning, our main results on TOFU and MUSE show a better balance between targeted forgetting and knowledge retention than the baselines, with retention performance close to the from-scratch retraining reference.

infographic.key_insight: CurvDelta restricts model updates to a low-curvature space to acquire or remove targeted capabilities while better preserving general capabilities.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a geometry-aware approach to LLM fine-tuning and selective unlearning when retaining existing capabilities is critical.
method: Analyze local preservation-loss geometry around the pre-adaptation model to identify low-curvature update directions.
Use Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC) and factorized projection to make the construction practical for LLMs.
Introduce CurvLoRA, a low-rank adaptation variant using the same preservation geometry.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports competitive math and code performance with better general-capability retention, plus improved forgetting–retention balance on TOFU and MUSE, with retention close to from-scratch retraining.
infographic.watch_item: Preservation relies on a local, approximate curvature model; robustness to large updates and curvature-estimation overhead should be checked in deployment.
infographic.paper_title: CurvDelta: Low-Curvature Delta Modeling For Surgical Learning and Unlearning

title: Infinity-Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Principal Component Analysis: Exact Reformulation, Finite-Sample Guarantee, and Efficient Algorithm
authors: Zhouxing Luo, Lei Wang, Xin Liu
abstract: Principal component analysis (PCA) is a fundamental and ubiquitous technique for dimension reduction and representation learning, yet its empirical formulation remains vulnerable to distributional uncertainty. While distributionally robust optimization (DRO) offers a natural remedy, existing order-2 Wasserstein models of PCA either preserve the nominal PCA subspace or lack an exact reformulation. This paper demonstrates how the infinity-Wasserstein distance can reconcile these two desirable properties. For the resulting DRO model of PCA, we derive an exact finite-dimensional reformulation and explicitly identify a worst-case distribution attaining the inner maximum. Crucially, the reformulated objective retains samplewise residual information beyond the empirical covariance matrix, revealing a mechanism through which distributional robustness can reshape the learned principal subspace. Under the mild assumption that the true distribution has a finite fourth moment, we further establish a uniform finite-sample performance guarantee for the proposed model. An iteratively reweighted majorization-minimization algorithm is also developed to solve the resulting nonconvex and nonsmooth optimization problem, with a rigorous analysis of its convergence properties. Numerical experiments substantiate the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithm and the practical effectiveness of the infinity-Wasserstein model in downstream applications.

infographic.key_insight: Infinity-Wasserstein robust PCA admits an exact finite-dimensional reformulation while retaining samplewise residual information that can reshape the learned principal subspace.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers a distributionally robust approach to dimensionality reduction and representation learning when the deployment distribution may differ from the empirical data.
method: Reformulate infinity-Wasserstein robust PCA exactly and explicitly construct a worst-case distribution.
Establish a uniform finite-sample performance guarantee assuming a finite fourth moment.
Solve the nonconvex, nonsmooth problem with iteratively reweighted majorization-minimization and analyze convergence.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments support computational efficiency and downstream effectiveness, but the abstract reports no datasets, baselines, or quantitative gains.
infographic.watch_item: The reformulated problem remains nonconvex, so the reported convergence analysis should not be read as a guarantee of global optimality.
infographic.paper_title: Infinity-Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Principal Component Analysis: Exact Reformulation, Finite-Sample Guarantee, and Efficient Algorithm

title: Stable admissible neural classes and convergent physics-informed neural networks
authors: Leevan Ling, Shu Ma, Yizhong Sun
abstract: Residual-based methods, including physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), physics-informed Kolmogorov--Arnold networks, and some physics-informed neural operator architectures, approximate PDE solutions by minimizing a discrete least-squares loss formed from the PDE and boundary residuals over a prescribed trial class. This structure is shared by classical least-squares Kansa collocation, whose kernel trial spaces admit an established convergence theory. For neural trial classes, approximation power alone does not ensure that discrete residuals control the continuous solution error. For linear elliptic Dirichlet problems, we extend the kernel-based collocation framework to neural trial classes through elliptic regularity, discrete stability, and consistency. Elliptic regularity supplies the PDE estimate relating solution error to continuous residuals. Discrete stability identifies admissible trial subclasses in which continuous residuals are controlled by a computable discrete loss. This step also quantifies the required number of collocation points. Furthermore, the stability analysis naturally demands a scale-dependent, physics-balanced boundary weight. For the constrained problem, consistency requires accurate comparison functions within the same admissible subclass, a requirement not supplied by neural approximation estimates alone. Specializing to multilayer perceptrons with tanh activations (tanh-MLPs), we construct admissible comparison networks and establish convergence for the constrained residual minimization problem. We further obtain conditional convergence of unconstrained physics-balanced PINNs based on tanh-MLPs under joint network and sampling refinement.

infographic.key_insight: For linear elliptic Dirichlet PDEs, neural approximation power alone does not guarantee PINN convergence: discrete stability and accurate comparison networks within admissible trial classes are also needed.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework guides collocation-point counts and scale-dependent, physics-balanced boundary weighting so sampled residual losses can control solution error.
method: Extend kernel collocation theory using elliptic regularity, discrete stability, and consistency.
Identify stable admissible neural subclasses and quantify their sampling requirements.
Construct admissible tanh-MLP comparison networks to prove constrained convergence and conditional unconstrained convergence.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical convergence results for tanh-MLPs, but no numerical benchmarks or empirical error measurements.
infographic.watch_item: Unconstrained PINN convergence remains conditional under joint network and sampling refinement; generic approximation guarantees alone are insufficient.
infographic.paper_title: Stable admissible neural classes and convergent physics-informed neural networks

title: A Survey on the Use of Machine Learning within Computer Algebra
authors: Uzma Shafiq, Matthew England, Nayyar Zaidi
abstract: This survey explores the use of Machine Learning (ML) in the field of Computer Algebra (CA), both to optimise existing CA algorithms, and to perform symbolic computation directly. Traditional symbolic methods, while mathematically rigorous, often are computationally expensive thus limiting their use in real-world applications. Recent advances have shown that data-driven techniques can address these limitations by guiding heuristic decisions, selecting optimal algorithms, predicting structural properties of algebraic objects, or even making direct symbolic computations. We take a systematic literature review approach and uncover work in CA applications including cylindrical algebraic decomposition, Gröbner basis computation, symbolic integration, and many more. The survey compares the different ML approaches that have been employed for these tasks, ranging from decision trees to transformers. Issues uncovered by the survey include the lack of benchmark datasets for CA, which hinders the comparison of methods and the generalizability of ML models. The survey identifies the potential for explainable AI tools to help develop trust in decisions, and to drive forward CA research itself.

infographic.key_insight: Machine learning can guide computer algebra algorithms and perform symbolic computations directly, offering ways to reduce computational cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: ML-guided heuristics and algorithm selection could make expensive symbolic computations more practical for engineering workflows.
method: Systematically review ML applications in computer algebra.
Cover cylindrical algebraic decomposition, Gröbner bases, symbolic integration, and other tasks.
Compare approaches ranging from decision trees to transformers.

infographic.watch_item: For direct symbolic computation, ML outputs require mathematical verification rather than being assumed correct.
infographic.paper_title: A Survey on the Use of Machine Learning within Computer Algebra

title: Regularized Score Centering
authors: Hao Bai, Chenlu Ye, Xuanchang Zhang, Aviral Kumar, Tong Zhang
abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning increases training throughput, but data from stale policies and numerical mismatch between training and inference can destabilize learning. To stabilize off-policy learning, score centering (SC) removes the effect of reward baselines on the expected update. Our gradient diagnostics show less extreme gradients with SC than with importance sampling (IS), but SC can still fail when the learner moves far from the behavior policy that generated the data. To limit this policy mismatch, we introduce Regularized Score Centering (RSC), which adds a reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty to encourage the learner's next-token distribution to stay close to the behavior policy's next-token distribution. RSC works with or without truncated importance sampling (TIS), which caps token importance weights. Our theoretical analysis supports this approach, showing that KL regularization improves convergence guarantees. We evaluate dense and mixture-of-experts models on mathematical reasoning and agentic tasks, including online shopping, tool use, games, and fully asynchronous software engineering. RSC with TIS substantially improves sample efficiency across all agentic benchmarks, attaining higher training rewards with the same number of sampled responses. In final evaluations, it achieves top performance across all six agentic tasks, improving by 14.3% on AppWorld and reaching 9.9 times the strongest baseline's score on BabyAI.

infographic.key_insight: Regularized Score Centering stabilizes off-policy reinforcement learning by combining score centering with a reverse-KL penalty that limits drift from the data-generating policy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: RSC targets instability from stale rollout data and training–inference numerical mismatch, making it relevant to high-throughput asynchronous training.
method: Use score centering to remove reward-baseline effects from the expected update.
Add reverse-KL regularization to keep learner next-token distributions close to the behavior policy.
Optionally apply truncated importance sampling to cap token importance weights.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations span dense and mixture-of-experts models on mathematical reasoning and agentic tasks; RSC with TIS leads across six agentic tasks, with a reported 14.3% AppWorld improvement and 9.9× the strongest baseline’s BabyAI score.
infographic.watch_item: KL strength and importance-weight truncation require care: excessive constraints may limit learning, while weak constraints may leave harmful policy mismatch.
infographic.paper_title: Regularized Score Centering

title: Second scaling regime in high-dimensional function approximation and curse of dimensionality
authors: Shukai Du, Thu Le, Samuel N. Stechmann
abstract: High-dimensional function approximation is often subject to the curse of dimensionality, commonly described by a hypercube scaling regime with a large expense of $R^d$ grid points, where $R$ denotes the side length of a hypercube in $d$ dimensions. Here we show that a second scaling regime, which we call the lattice ball scaling regime, also arises and is relevant for practical applications. In this regime, the expense scales as $d^{R^2}/(R^2!)$ and therefore grows polynomially with $d$. This regime arises without additional special assumptions of special types of function spaces or error norms. The lattice ball scaling regime occurs when $R^2\ll d$, due to the discrete nature of counting the expense as the number of lattice points inside a hypersphere. Here we investigate this regime, which arises from the classical problem of approximating high-dimensional functions from common spaces of analytic or $m$-times continuously differentiable functions using orthogonal series (spectral method) such as Fourier, Chebyshev, and Legendre polynomial series. For many applications, the expense in the lattice ball scaling regime can be substantially smaller than that of the hypercube scaling regime, making accurate approximations more accessible. Numerical illustrations include classifying images of handwritten digits from the MNIST dataset and learning the solution operators of partial differential equations, such as Burgers' equation and the radiative transfer equation. The potential for connections with artificial neural networks and other machine learning methods is also discussed.

infographic.key_insight: High-dimensional function approximation has a lattice-ball regime with expense scaling as d^(R²)/(R²!), polynomial in dimension d for fixed R, when R² ≪ d.
infographic.engineering_relevance: In this regime, spectral approximations can require substantially fewer terms than the conventional R^d hypercube scaling suggests.
method: Approximate analytic or m-times continuously differentiable functions using Fourier, Chebyshev, or Legendre series.
Count spectral indices as lattice points inside a high-dimensional ball.
Identify the second scaling regime arising from discrete lattice-point counting.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical illustrations cover MNIST digit classification and learning solution operators for Burgers’ and radiative transfer equations.
infographic.watch_item: The favorable scaling depends on R² ≪ d and does not establish polynomial cost when R must grow with dimension or accuracy requirements.
infographic.paper_title: Second scaling regime in high-dimensional function approximation and curse of dimensionality

title: Zonotopic Analysis of Quantization Error in Neural Networks
authors: Robert Debbas, Éric Goubault, Sylvie Putot
abstract: Quantized neural networks achieve computational efficiency by reducing precision, but bounding their quantization error remains a challenge due to discrete rounding and clamping operations. We present a zonotope-based abstract interpretation framework for quantized ReLU feed-forward network verification, introducing a unified round-clamp abstract transformer that jointly handles both operations. We extend this framework to constrained zonotopes, which add linear constraints to tighten bounds, and derive sound quantization error representations. We establish soundness and affine-strip optimality of the round-clamp abstract transformer, as well as convex-hull optimality of its complete constrained formulation. On the ACAS Xu benchmarks, our constrained zonotope method reduces average error-bound widths by approximately 70-85% and runtimes by 65-80% compared to QEBVerif's symbolic DRA propagation at the two smallest tested perturbation radii (r=3 and r=6). These improvements are not uniform across bitwidths, and symbolic DRA achieves tighter bounds at larger radii. Our plain zonotope method delivers competitive sound bounds nearly 300 times faster on average.

infographic.key_insight: A unified round-clamp transformer enables sound zonotopic bounds on neural-network quantization error, with linear constraints tightening the analysis.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework can accelerate quantized ReLU network verification while providing mathematically sound error bounds.
method: Model rounding and clamping jointly using a zonotope abstract transformer.
Add linear constraints through constrained zonotopes to tighten error bounds.
Prove soundness, affine-strip optimality, and convex-hull optimality for the complete constrained formulation.

infographic.watch_item: Gains vary across bitwidths, and symbolic DRA produces tighter bounds at larger perturbation radii.
infographic.paper_title: Zonotopic Analysis of Quantization Error in Neural Networks

title: LProp: Propagating Latent Uncertainty through Evidence-Conditioned Belief Revision in LLM Agents
authors: Kaiwen Shi, Zheyuan Zhang, Weixiang Sun, Han Bao, Colby Nelson, Yanfang Ye
abstract: When LLM agents pass intermediate judgments downstream without uncertainty, later decisions may treat tentative assumptions as facts. Effective uncertainty propagation must preserve information for correction and update inherited beliefs as new evidence arrives. Yet scalar scores omit information needed for revision, while detailed descriptions and reflection incur additional costs. We introduce Latent Uncertainty, a latent-space estimator that preserves uncertainty-relevant information without lengthy descriptions. Building on this, we propose LProp (Latent Uncertainty Propagation), which revises inherited answer distributions using latent representations and new evidence without additional trajectory sampling. We evaluate both methods across multiple-choice, yes/no, open-ended question answering, and mathematical reasoning tasks. Our approach outperforms baselines on most metrics, while LProp achieves the lowest mean inference-token usage in all eight propagation settings. Matched feature ablations further demonstrate that inherited latent content improves error recovery beyond answer probabilities or model capacity alone.

infographic.key_insight: LProp propagates uncertainty through latent representations, allowing downstream LLM agents to revise inherited beliefs rather than treat tentative judgments as facts.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a token-efficient way to support belief correction in multi-stage LLM workflows without additional trajectory sampling.
method: Estimate uncertainty in latent space without lengthy textual descriptions.
Revise inherited answer distributions using latent representations and new evidence.
Preserve uncertainty-relevant information beyond scalar scores or answer probabilities.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across multiple-choice, yes/no, open-ended QA, and mathematical reasoning evaluations, the approach outperforms baselines on most metrics; LProp uses the fewest mean inference tokens in all eight propagation settings, and matched ablations support latent content’s contribution to error recovery.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment may require access to model-internal representations; the abstract does not establish compatibility with black-box LLM APIs.
infographic.paper_title: LProp: Propagating Latent Uncertainty through Evidence-Conditioned Belief Revision in LLM Agents

title: Stochastic Representation-Inspired Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Incompressible Fluid Flows
authors: Zihao Guo, Zhongmin Qian
abstract: The effectiveness of neural networks in solving partial differential equations depends not only on their approximation capability but also on the suitability of their representations for the underlying solutions. Motivated by stochastic integral representations of incompressible fluid flows and the associated Biot--Savart kernel, we propose a Biot--Savart-informed (i.e. physics-informed) neural network (BS-PINN) for the incompressible Navier--Stokes equations. By extracting a rational profile from a regularized Biot--Savart kernel, we construct a smooth activation function with fixed and learnable kernel scales. Both variants retain the conventional velocity--pressure formulation and physics-informed training framework, allowing the influence of the activation function to be examined independently. We evaluate the method on five benchmarks, including Kovasznay flow, cylinder wake, three-dimensional Beltrami flow, Taylor--Green vortex, and double shear layer. Across 21 benchmark--architecture comparisons, both variants consistently reduce the combined velocity error relative to the conventional $\tanh$-based PINN, achieving mean relative error reductions of 31.7\% and 33.2\%, respectively. Improvements are also observed in reported pressure and vorticity errors. Notably, the double-shear-layer experiments demonstrate improved resolution of localized shear structures and, for BS-PINN-F, qualitatively clearer vortex-roll-up patterns in the long-time simulation. These findings highlight the potential of incorporating analytical flow structures into neural-network representations for incompressible flow simulations.

infographic.key_insight: A smooth activation inspired by the regularized Biot–Savart kernel improves incompressible-flow PINN accuracy without changing the velocity–pressure formulation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Physics-informed activation design offers a targeted way to improve neural fluid simulations, including resolution of localized shear structures.
method: Extract a rational activation profile from a regularized Biot–Savart kernel.
Test fixed-scale and learnable-scale activation variants.
Retain conventional velocity–pressure outputs and physics-informed training.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 21 benchmark–architecture comparisons spanning five flow benchmarks, the fixed- and learnable-scale variants reduced combined velocity error versus tanh PINNs by mean values of 31.7% and 33.2%, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish computational-cost savings or generalization beyond the five tested flow benchmarks.
infographic.paper_title: Stochastic Representation-Inspired Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Incompressible Fluid Flows

title: MCTS Is Counting the Wrong Thing: Learning Exploration Counts for LLM Reasoning
authors: Xuan Zhang, Zhijian Zhou, Zicheng Hu, Yan Feng, Hongyan Hao, Yuan Qi
abstract: Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) has powered landmark successes in reinforcement learning, yet its gains in LLM reasoning can remain modest despite substantial search effort. We identify an overlooked bottleneck: what MCTS counts. Standard UCT assigns independent visit counts to textual branches, allowing different formulations of the same reasoning strategy to repeatedly receive exploration bonuses. Our theoretical analysis shows that this count fragmentation can impair exploration efficiency, as quantified by increased cumulative regret. To address this problem, we introduce Learned Pseudo-Count MCTS (LPC-MCTS), which changes only the exploration statistic in UCT. A lightweight Coin-Flipping Network head on the policy's hidden representations estimates representation coverage, enabling related branches to share exploration evidence. Across 5 mathematical-reasoning and 7 search benchmarks, LPC-MCTS consistently outperforms strong MCTS baselines. Holding each LPC-MCTS-trained policy fixed, replacing standard MCTS counts at inference improves average mean@16 accuracy across 5 mathematical benchmarks by 3.79 percentage points on Qwen2.5-7B and 2.71 points on Qwen3-4B. Applying LPC-MCTS during both training and inference yields gains of 4.96 and 4.37 points over standard MCTS, respectively. Together, our theory and experiments show that changing what MCTS counts can substantially improve its exploration efficiency and reasoning performance.

infographic.key_insight: MCTS can waste exploration on differently worded versions of the same reasoning strategy; learned pseudo-counts let related branches share exploration evidence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Changing only UCT’s exploration statistic offers a targeted way to improve LLM reasoning search without redesigning the full search algorithm.
method: Identify how fragmented branch visit counts can increase cumulative regret.
Estimate representation coverage with a lightweight Coin-Flipping Network head on policy hidden states.
Use learned pseudo-counts in UCT to share exploration evidence across related branches.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 5 mathematical-reasoning and 7 search benchmarks, LPC-MCTS outperformed strong MCTS baselines; with trained policies held fixed, inference-time count replacement improved average mean@16 math accuracy by 3.79 percentage points on Qwen2.5-7B and 2.71 on Qwen3-4B.
infographic.watch_item: Coverage estimates depend on learned representations; the abstract does not quantify the head’s computational overhead or robustness to misleading branch similarity.
infographic.paper_title: MCTS Is Counting the Wrong Thing: Learning Exploration Counts for LLM Reasoning

title: Large Language Models as Nonlinear Dynamical Systems: The Three Clocks of Depth, Training, and Generation
authors: Maor Farid
abstract: Language models are dynamical systems. A transformer is iterated over its layers, over the steps of its training and over the tokens it generates, and on each of these three clocks it shows behavior that nonlinear dynamics has studied for a century: fixed points, bifurcations, synchronization, chaos and noise-driven escape from potential wells. The two communities rarely meet, so this behavior is often rediscovered under new names. We build a bridge between them. To describe, we condense about 200 papers into the Three-Clock Dictionary, which maps fifteen concepts of nonlinear dynamics onto each clock and marks every correspondence as proved, measured or conjectured, and we show each concept in a mechanical system and in a language model side by side. To explain, we derive reduced-order models: the softmax is a Boltzmann distribution, gradient descent an Euler step on a nonlinear spring, a loss spike a ball thrown out of a stiff valley, attention on the circle a Kuramoto model, and a repetition loop a well that deepens while it is occupied. We then test these explanations on open language models, on a laptop CPU. Escape from repetition loops in GPT-2 and Pythia follows the Arrhenius law with the logit gap as the barrier, and the barrier deepens and then saturates, so the temperature needed to leave a loop falls like $1/\ln N$ with the generation length $N$ and rises with model size. Coherent text lives in a narrow window of temperatures, which a small reasoning model shares at its recommended temperature. Training makes each Pythia layer more expansive, and a small transformer trains at a multi-mode edge of stability. The third step, solving problems of language models, is still ahead: controllers derived from the escape analysis remove loops but do not yet beat the best fixed temperature. We state twelve open problems where nonlinear dynamics could get there.

infographic.key_insight: Language models exhibit nonlinear dynamics across three clocks—layer depth, training steps, and token generation—with repetition-loop escape following an Arrhenius law.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Dynamical-systems models offer interpretable tools for studying training stability and generation temperature, though adaptive loop control has not yet outperformed the best fixed temperature.
method: Synthesize about 200 papers into a Three-Clock Dictionary mapping 15 concepts, with correspondences labeled proved, measured, or conjectured.
Derive reduced-order models linking softmax, gradient descent, attention, and repetition to physical dynamics.
Test predictions on open language models and a small transformer using a laptop CPU.
infographic.evidence_signal: GPT-2 and Pythia experiments support Arrhenius repetition-loop escape with logit-gap barriers; Pythia layers become more expansive during training, and a small transformer trains at a multi-mode edge of stability.
infographic.watch_item: The framework mixes established results with conjectures, and loop-removal controllers do not yet beat the best fixed-temperature baseline.
infographic.paper_title: Large Language Models as Nonlinear Dynamical Systems: The Three Clocks of Depth, Training, and Generation

title: Efficient Variance-Aware Reinforcement Learning in Time-Inhomogeneous Linear MDPs
authors: Qingyue Zhao, Qiwei Di, Jiafan He, Heyang Zhao, Kaixuan Ji, Quanquan Gu
abstract: We study variance-dependent reinforcement learning in episodic time-inhomogeneous linear Markov decision processes (MDPs) with feature dimension $d$, horizon $H$, and $K$ episodes. While recent works have established variance-dependent regret with $\tilde{O}(1)$ deterministic-regime overhead for linear mixture MDPs (Zhao et al., 2023) and worst-case nearly minimax optimal regret $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H^3 K} + d^7 H^8)$ for linear MDPs (He et al., 2023),, existing variance-aware analyses for linear MDPs (Li and Sun, 2023; Huang et al., 2023) rely on a coarse concentration step whose resulting regret guarantees retain a polynomial $\tilde{O}(K^{1/4})$ additive term even in deterministic environments. We propose VA-LSVI-UCB++, a computationally efficient algorithm that achieves the variance-dependent regret bound $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H\min\{\mathrm{Var}_K^*,\mathrm{Var}_K^π\}}+d^5H^4)$, where $\mathrm{Var}_K^*$ and $\mathrm{Var}_K^π$ denote the cumulative conditional variances of the optimal value function and the played policies' value functions along the realized trajectory. Our result adapts to the minimum of the two realized trajectory variances, recovers the worst-case minimax optimal leading term $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H^3 K})$, and collapses to $\tilde{O}(d^5 H^4)$ in deterministic environments, free of polynomial-in-$K$ dependency. At the core of our analysis is a simultaneous three-way reference-advantage decomposition for the optimistic, pessimistic, and squared value function estimators coupled with variance self-bounding and Freedman-type value-difference arguments, which tightens the pessimistic and second-moment confidence radii by a factor of $\tilde{O}(d H)$ and removes the inverse-variance-floor blowup.

infographic.key_insight: VA-LSVI-UCB++ achieves variance-adaptive regret Õ(d√(H min{Var_K*, Var_K^π}) + d⁵H⁴), eliminating polynomial dependence on episode count K in deterministic environments.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For systems modeled as episodic time-inhomogeneous linear MDPs, the algorithm offers computationally efficient learning guarantees that improve when trajectory uncertainty is low.
method: Decompose optimistic, pessimistic, and squared value estimators simultaneously into reference and advantage terms.
Combine variance self-bounding with Freedman-type value-difference arguments.
Tighten pessimistic and second-moment confidence radii by an Õ(dH) factor.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical regret guarantees, including a minimax-optimal worst-case leading term Õ(d√(H³K)), but no empirical evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantee assumes a linear MDP model, and the additive Õ(d⁵H⁴) term may be substantial for large feature dimensions or horizons.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Variance-Aware Reinforcement Learning in Time-Inhomogeneous Linear MDPs

title: Transferring an analysis of human brain organization to language models
authors: Donghyeok Lee, Sangwon Yu, Sangkwon Park, Hye Youn Park, Munyoung Chang, Sungroh Yoon
abstract: During human cortical development, functional systems become increasingly differentiated. We asked whether improved reasoning in language models involves a comparable regional reorganization. Applying diffusion-map embedding, used to characterize cortical organization, to matched base and reasoning-trained models from three families, we found broadly preserved gradient profiles with localized changes within a contiguous layer span. Grafting weights from these spans into instruction-tuned hosts improved mathematical reasoning on average, with gains rising with region overlap, while retaining more previously solved problems than grafts elsewhere. Across training, the span formed gradually during the early rise in performance, and grafts from intermediate stages helped. Grafts shifted most hosts partly towards their donors' behaviour and sometimes improved on problems the donors failed; the same analysis located a transferable span in a medical model. Together, these findings identify a reasoning-related region whose weights improve reasoning with low interference in the host's existing mathematical competence.

infographic.key_insight: A brain-inspired analysis identifies a contiguous layer span whose weights can improve language-model reasoning while largely preserving existing mathematical competence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Targeted weight grafting offers a way to transfer reasoning gains into instruction-tuned hosts without replacing the entire model.
method: Apply diffusion-map embedding to matched base and reasoning-trained models from three families.
Locate contiguous layer spans with localized changes in otherwise preserved gradient profiles.
Graft weights from these spans into instruction-tuned hosts and evaluate mathematical reasoning and retention.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three model families, targeted grafts improved mathematical reasoning on average, with gains increasing with region overlap and better retention of previously solved problems than grafts elsewhere.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify gains or establish whether the identified spans generalize beyond the studied model families and evaluations.
infographic.paper_title: Transferring an analysis of human brain organization to language models
